analysis.one_liner: Curb ATF enforcement against licensed gun dealers, seal gun-trace data, and stiffen penalties for armed felons.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 224 cosponsors—more than half the House—but died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how the ATF polices licensed gun dealers: civil fines would be capped, license revocations would get review hearings, and a dealer could only be penalized for knowingly and deliberately ignoring a known legal duty. It would also seal the ATF's firearms trace database from cities and civil lawsuits, allow gun makers and federal security contractors to possess machineguns for work purposes, ban fees for background checks, and let minors use handguns with a parent present without prior written permission. On the other side of the ledger, it would raise prison sentences for felons with violent or serious drug convictions who are caught with guns.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal firearms licensees (gun dealers) gain the most: capped fines, a stiffer standard for enforcement, five-year limits on prosecution, the right to keep operating and sell off inventory after a license is revoked or surrendered, and guaranteed hearings before any denial or penalty takes effect. Gun manufacturers and importers gain new legal access to machineguns for testing, training, and security contracts, plus easier importation of barrels and receivers. Private security contractors with federal contracts gain the right to possess machineguns. Rank-and-file gun buyers gain the elimination of any background-check fee and simpler rules for supervised handgun use by minors. Motion picture and television firearms dealers gain a new theatrical machinegun exception.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun dealers, manufacturers, and security contractors

how_it_helps.text: Caps civil penalties for dealer violations at $1,000 per minor violation (max $5,000 per inspection) and $2,500 per serious violation (max $15,000 per inspection), replacing what could previously be outright license revocation for willful violations.

Redefines 'willfully' so a dealer can only be penalized for a violation if they knew of a legal duty and knowingly and intentionally disregarded it, and bars enforcement more than five years after a violation.

Lets a dealer whose license is expired, surrendered, or revoked keep operating and sell off inventory for 60 days, unless a court finds by clear and convincing evidence the business is an immediate and grave public-safety threat.

Requires the Attorney General to give license applicants written notice and reasons for a proposed denial, with a hearing at a location convenient to the applicant, and stays any penalty while review is pending.
Bans any tax or fee for the National Instant Criminal Background Check System, so buyers pay nothing for a background check.
Removes the prior written permission requirement for a minor under 18 to use a handgun for target practice, hunting, or safety instruction when a parent or guardian is present at all times.

Raises penalties under the armed-career-criminal provision: up to 15 years for one prior violent or serious drug conviction, up to 20 for two, and at least 15 years to life, with no probation or suspended sentence, for three.

analysis.who_pays: Communities affected by crime guns would bear the cost if the bill passed: the same dealer-inspection regime that can shut down businesses funneling guns to prohibited buyers would carry capped fines and a much higher bar for enforcement. Cities would lose access to the ATF trace database for civil suits and could not use trace information in litigation, because the database would be immune from subpoenas and discovery. Law enforcement and researchers would lose access to trace data and to name-based retrieval of records on dealers no longer licensed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Crime-gun victims and cities suing over traces

drawbacks.text: The penalty caps and the new knowledge-based 'willfully' standard would make it substantially harder for ATF to fine or revoke the small share of dealers who transfer guns to prohibited purchasers, which is how many crime guns reach the street.

Locking the firearms trace database away from anyone but prosecutors and intelligence officials—and making it immune from subpoenas in civil cases—would block cities that sue dealers and independent researchers from using trace data to show how guns move from licensed sellers to crime scenes.

Expanding legal machinegun possession to federal security contractors and manufacturers for testing, training, and theatrical use would add machineguns to the civilian stream of commerce, even with the bill's periodic background checks and Attorney General authorization requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine public benefits are modest and real: no fee for a background check, higher sentences for repeat armed felons, and a written-report requirement for state agencies that store explosives. But the core of the bill is enforcement relief for licensed gun dealers—capped fines, a stiffer intent standard, post-revocation selling rights, and a sealed trace database. For a reader weighing this honestly, the dealer protections and trace-data lockdown are the heart of the bill, and they come at the cost of weaker oversight of the businesses through which crime guns most often flow.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in December 2007 and then to its Crime subcommittee in January 2008, and it never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King (R-IA) introduced the bill on December 19, 2007, joined by Rep. Zack Space (D-OH).
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, for parts within its jurisdiction, to the Ways and Means Committee.
On January 14, 2008, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill accumulated 224 cosponsors—168 Republicans and 56 Democrats—yet died in subcommittee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Licensed gun dealers and firearms manufacturers are better off because the bill died: ATF kept operating under the existing, tougher enforcement rules rather than the bill's penalty caps, five-year enforcement limits, and post-revocation selling rights, and the trace database remained available for litigation and research.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers and ATF's existing oversight

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: Rep. Zack Space
for.what_they_did: Joined King in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

for.name: National Rifle Association
for.what_they_did: Backed ATF reform legislation of this kind; the bill's dealer-penalty and trace-data provisions track the group's long-standing model language.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chairman John Conyers (D-MI) controlled its markup calendar
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Crime subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or floor vote during the 14 months it had the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican—168 of 202 House Republicans and 56 of 233 House Democrats signed on—so support skewed strongly toward one party, though it fell well short of the full Republican conference and never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill caps fines for dealer violations, raises the intent standard for enforcement, limits enforcement to five years, and lets revoked dealers keep selling for 60 days. The public cost is weaker oversight of the businesses through which guns are transferred to prohibited buyers; the dealer's gain comes directly from that loss of enforcement.

New legal access to machineguns for testing, research, training, and theatrical use, easier importation of barrels and receivers, and a narrower definition of manufacturing. These are commercial privileges carved out of the machinegun ban, with the main safeguard being periodic background checks.

Companies holding contracts to provide national security services for the federal government could possess machineguns for that work. This is closely tied to a government function but expands machinegun possession beyond law enforcement and the military.

The trace database would be off limits to everyone except prosecutors and intelligence officials, and immune from subpoenas in civil cases. Cities that sue dealers over crime-gun flows, and researchers studying where crime guns come from, would lose their main source of trace data.

A narrow exception would let qualifying motion-picture firearms businesses possess machineguns for productions, with registration, state licensing, income, and documentation requirements. A niche commercial gain with little public-safety downside.

No fee or tax for the national background check, and no written permission needed for a minor to use a handgun under a parent's direct supervision. Small direct consumer benefits that run alongside the public's interest.
